newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's unlikely little heroes slurp ice lollies.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's unlikely little heroes slurp ice lollies.

text.p: Most conquering armies expect an ice cold beer when they take a town. Zaire's unlikely little heroes settled gladly on Thursday for purple ice lollies.
The disciplined column of boy soldiers, who entered Zaire's second city from the south as part of the advancing rebel forces of Laurent Kabila, looked no more than 14 or 15 years old.

They were bringing up the rear after the city was secured, but they were thronged as liberators by ecstatic swarms of people chanting the name of Kabila. And they marched on in, upfront, like battle-hardened soldiers.
They were not inclined to answer questions about their age, but they rubbed their stomachs and rolled their eyes in the universal sign-language denoting hunger, and they were obviously parched.
They said they had marched a long, long way, toting AK-47 automatic rifles and other serious weapons, plus kit.

Their boots and their camouflage uniforms were dusty but their caps were on straight -- until the ice lollipops appeared and their youth shone suddenly through, like a ray of innocence behind the hard stares of war.
Purple juice trickled down off tilted throats as they sucked greedily at plastic bags of sugared ice handed to them by grateful wellwishers.
They smacked their lips and wiped their mouths on the backs of boyish black forearms in an ecstasy of slaked thirst that no television cola commercial could equal.

In stark contrast to their still bashful faces were the hand grenades pinned to their junior size tunic fronts and the heavy bandoliers of brass-jacketed bullets that some carried about their shoulders.
The use of boys in their teens in warfare could no doubt prove controversial for Zaire's rebel army, as it has done in previous African conflicts where the young have been given guns.
Yet it will be hard to argue with success, or with the heroes' welcome these boys received as the liberators of Lubumbashi.

Judging by the momentum of the past few weeks in Kabila's war to oust President Mobutu Sese Seko they will gain a place in the history of how Zaire finally overthrew three decades of corrupt dictatorship.
But on Thursday they remained anonymous, and no one seemed certain even about which country they came from. They were hungry, and thirsty, and brave and young.
